os-efcore.title: Data with EF Core
os-efcore.summary: Everything your app needs around EF Core, done once: saves that tell you what happened instead of throwing, who-and-when columns filled in for you, soft delete, change history, paging, batch work and transactions that do not lose data. You add one database package next to it: SQLite, SQL Server, PostgreSQL or MySQL.

gives.1: Every save answers with an `OSResult`: how many rows were added, changed and deleted, or a clear code such as `data.duplicate` with the field that caused it. No database exception reaches your screen.
gives.2: Created by, changed by, deleted by and their times are filled in on every save. Delete can keep the row as deleted, and a full change history is one line away.
gives.3: Paging that stays fast on big tables, batch updates that do not lock the database for minutes, and transactions that retry safely and never half-save.

sample.register: Set up the data layer once
sample.page: Show one page of a list

start.title: Start here
start.summary: A short walk from an empty project to saving, paging and handling an error, and which database package to pick.

1.title: Pick a package
1.text: Choose the database package by where your data lives.

2.title: Same steps
2.text: Entities, a context, one `AddOS...` call, then migrations.

3.title: Save and page
3.text: Use `SaveAsync` and `PageAsync`, and check `Code` on errors.

4.title: Reviewable SQL
4.text: `dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent` gives SQL you can read before it runs.

1.title: Which package
1.text:
OS.EFCore is the shared part; a database package does the database-specific part. Pick the package by where your data lives.

SQLite: a single file next to the app, no server, ideal for desktop apps, small services and tests; it can encrypt the whole file.

SQL Server or Azure SQL: the usual choice for company systems; real-server tests ran on LocalDB.

PostgreSQL: a free, strong server database; tested with unit tests only so far.

MySQL: when MySQL is already in place; today it runs on Oracle's provider (GPL with an open-source exception) and has unit tests only.

2.title: The steps
2.text:
The steps are the same everywhere. Write your entities, deriving from `TrackedEntity` or `StampedEntity` when you want the who-and-when columns. Write a context that derives from `OSDbContext`.

One call to `AddOSSqlite`, `AddOSSqlServer`, `AddOSPostgres` or `AddOSMySql` is enough, because it registers OS.EFCore too. Add `AddOSEFCore` only to change shared settings, before or after the provider.

3.title: Schema and saving
3.text:
Create the schema with the normal EF tools: `dotnet ef migrations add Initial`. For production, `dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent` gives SQL you can review before it runs.

Then save with `SaveAsync`, page with `PageAsync` and look at the result's `Code` when something goes wrong. The samples below show the real output of each step.

register.title: Set up the data layer
register.note: In a real app you would use `AddOSSqlite` (or another database package) instead of `UseSqlite`; it does the same plus the database's own settings.

first-save.title: Your first save, and what comes back
first-save.note: `Demo.Open()` opens a throwaway in-memory database with the same setup as a real app, so the output below is real.

first-error.title: What happens when a save fails
first-error.note: The name is unique, so the second save fails. Nothing is thrown: you get `Conflict`, the code `data.duplicate` and a trace id for the logs.

first-page.title: Show one page of a list
first-page.note: The sort name usually comes from the screen. An unknown name is ignored, and the key is added so the order is always the same.

type.EFCoreEx: Registration, model switches and small helpers.
type.EFCoreOptions: Settings shared by every context in the app.

EFCoreEx.AddOSEFCore: Registers the shared options and the save pipeline. The database packages call it for you, so you need it only to change settings or to use `AddOSDbContext` directly. It is safe to call more than once, in any order: every call updates the same options, so a later call wins only for the values it sets.
EFCoreEx.AddOSDbContext: Registers a context with your own provider setup; the database packages call it for you. Pooled by default. Throws if `AddOSEFCore` was not called first; the database packages never hit this, because they register the core themselves.
EFCoreEx.UseOS: Applies the OS.EFCore setup (save pipeline, no-tracking queries, timeouts) to a builder you made yourself, for tools and tests.
EFCoreEx.Audit: Turns on the change history for one entity. Needs `ApplyAudit` in the model.
EFCoreEx.Versioned: Adds a `Version` Guid that changes on every save, so two people editing the same row are noticed.
EFCoreEx.KeepText: Keeps one text property exactly as given, skipping `NormalizeText`.
EFCoreEx.IgnoreSoftDelete: Shows soft-deleted rows in this one query.
EFCoreEx.Find: Picks a connection row by name (ignoring case and spaces), or the main row, or the first valid one. Null if nothing matches.

EFCoreOptions.AppCode: A short name of your app, written into every history row so you can tell apps apart in a shared database. At most 50 characters.
EFCoreOptions.MigrateOnStart: Applies pending migrations when the app starts. Off by default: several instances starting together should not race to change the schema.
EFCoreOptions.HistoryTable: A different name for EF's migrations history table.
EFCoreOptions.HistorySchema: The schema of that table. Needs `HistoryTable`.
EFCoreOptions.NormalizeText: A function applied to every text value you save, for example to turn Arabic ي and ك into Persian ی and ک. Values are also trimmed. Off when null.
EFCoreOptions.MaxPageSize: The largest page anyone can ask for, so a request for a million rows gets 200. 200 by default.
EFCoreOptions.RetryCount: How many times the server packages retry a temporary failure. 3 by default; 0 turns retries off.
EFCoreOptions.RetryDelay: The longest wait between two retries. 5 seconds by default.
EFCoreOptions.CommandTimeout: How long one database command may run before it gives up. 15 seconds by default.
EFCoreOptions.UseRelationalNulls: Compares nulls the database way instead of the C# way. Off by default.
EFCoreOptions.SlowTransactionThreshold: A transaction slower than this is logged as a warning with its name and time. 2 seconds by default.

context.title: Your context
context.summary: Derive from `OSDbContext`, read with `Entity`, change with `ForUpdate`, and save with `SaveAsync`.

1.title: Reading and changing
1.text: `Entity<T>()` reads fast; `ForUpdate<T>()` loads to change.

2.title: Save result
2.text: `Save` returns an `OSResult<SaveCounts>` with counts or an error code.

3.title: Partial save
3.text: `Patch` saves only the fields you name.

4.title: Read-only guard
4.text: A context with `IReadOnlyContext` throws on any save.

1.title: Reading and changing
1.text:
Your context derives from `OSDbContext` and configures entities as usual. Queries do not track what they return, which keeps reading fast.

Use `Entity<T>()` to read and `ForUpdate<T>()` when you load something to change it. If you change an entity you read with `Entity<T>()`, nothing is saved, because nobody is watching it.

2.title: Save results
2.text:
`Save` and `SaveAsync` return `OSResult<SaveCounts>`: `data.saved` with the counts, `data.unchanged` when there was nothing to save, or an error code.

When a form sends an object back, `Patch` saves only the fields you name and leaves the rest alone.

3.title: Protected and background
3.text:
A context that also implements `IReadOnlyContext` throws on any save, which protects report or replica contexts from accidental writes.

Background jobs that have no request scope open a context with `IDbFactory<TContext>` and dispose it themselves.

4.title: Shared options
4.text: The server packages share one options base, `DbServerOptions<TBuilder>`, so connection string, encryption and retry work the same way everywhere.

model.title: A context with one audited, versioned entity
model.note: `ApplyAudit` adds the history table. Leave it out if no entity calls `Audit()`.

edit.title: Load, change and save
edit.note: `ForUpdate` turns change tracking on for this query only.

patch.title: Save only what the form sent
patch.note: Only `Name` was saved. `Code` kept its value even though the form sent null.

read-only.title: A context that can never write
read-only.note: This is a programming mistake, so it throws instead of returning a result.

factory.title: Open a context in a background job
factory.note: The job owns the context, so it disposes it.

connections.title: Pick a connection from settings by name
connections.note: `ToString` shows only the name, so a password in a connection string does not end up in a log by accident.

type.OSDbContext: The base context: saving, paging, batch work and transactions.
type.IDbFactory{TContext}: Opens a context where there is no request scope.
type.IReadOnlyContext: Marks a context that must never save.
type.SaveCounts: How many rows one save added, changed and deleted.
type.DbConnectionEntry: One named connection string from your settings.
type.DbServerOptions{TBuilder}: Shared connection settings of the server database packages.

OSDbContext.Entity: The table of an entity for reading. Nothing is tracked.
OSDbContext.ForUpdate: A tracked query, for entities you will change and save.
OSDbContext.Patch: Marks only the named properties as changed, attaching the entity if needed. Throws if you name none.
OSDbContext.Save: Saves and returns the counts, `data.unchanged` or an error code. Known database errors never throw.
OSDbContext.SaveAsync: Saves and returns the counts, `data.unchanged` or an error code. Known database errors never throw.
OSDbContext.TranAsync: Runs several steps as one unit that commits only on success. See Transactions.
OSDbContext.PageAsync: Reads one page by number, with or without a total. See Paging.
OSDbContext.PageAfterAsync: Reads the page after a cursor. See Paging.
OSDbContext.StreamAsync: Reads every row in batches without tracking. See Paging.
OSDbContext.BatchDeleteAsync: Deletes matching rows in batches of 1000. See Batch work.
OSDbContext.BatchSoftDeleteAsync: Soft deletes matching rows in batches of 1000.
OSDbContext.BatchUpdateAsync: Updates matching rows in batches of 1000.
OSDbContext.Dispose: Releases the context and forgets its request scope; a pooled context goes back to the pool.
OSDbContext.DisposeAsync: Releases the context and forgets its request scope; a pooled context goes back to the pool.

IDbFactory{TContext}.Open: Opens a context bound to the current scope. Dispose it when you are done.
IDbFactory{TContext}.OpenAsync: Opens a context bound to the current scope. Dispose it when you are done.

DbConnectionEntry.Name: The name you look the connection up by.
DbConnectionEntry.Connection: The connection string. Keep it in user secrets or environment variables, not in source.
DbConnectionEntry.IsMain: Marks the connection used when no name is given.
DbConnectionEntry.IsValid: True when both name and connection are filled in.
DbConnectionEntry.ToString: Only the name, never the connection string.

DbServerOptions{TBuilder}.ConnectionString: The connection string. Required; a broken one is rejected without echoing it.
DbServerOptions{TBuilder}.Encrypt: Requires an encrypted connection. On by default; turn it off only for development.
DbServerOptions{TBuilder}.RetryOnFailure: Uses the database's retry strategy for temporary failures. On by default; the count comes from `EFCoreOptions.RetryCount`.

entities.title: Who and when, filled in for you
entities.summary: Pick the stamp columns an entity needs; creator, editor, deleter and their times are written on every save.

1.title: Stamp interfaces
1.text: Add an interface and the save fills who and when.

2.title: Soft delete
2.text: `ISoftDelete` keeps the row and hides it from queries.

3.title: UTC and user
3.text: Times come from `TimeProvider`, the user from `IDataActor`.

4.title: Safe create stamp
4.text: A create stamp can never be overwritten.

1.title: The interfaces
1.text:
Most tables need to know who created a row, who changed it last and when. Instead of setting these by hand, give the entity the matching interface and the save fills them in.

`ICreateStamp` adds `CreateDate` and `CreateBy`, `IModifyStamp` adds `ModifiedDate` and `ModifiedBy`, and `ISoftDelete` adds `IsDeleted`, `DeletedDate` and `DeletedBy`.

`IStamped` is create plus modify and `ITracked` is all three; the base classes `StampedEntity` and `TrackedEntity` already hold the properties. When tables are created, stamp columns go after your own columns.

2.title: Time and user
2.text:
Times are UTC from `TimeProvider`. The user comes from `IDataActor`, a small class your app registers as scoped; it is read when you save, so pooled contexts never mix users.

If no `IDataActor` is registered, the user columns stay empty; nothing fails.

3.title: Create stamp and soft delete
3.text:
A create stamp cannot be overwritten: even if the code or a form sets `CreateBy`, the old value stays.

Removing an entity with `ISoftDelete` keeps the row and marks it deleted, and every query hides deleted rows until you ask with `IgnoreSoftDelete()`.

entities.title: Two entities with stamps
entities.note: `TrackedEntity` gives create, modify and soft delete stamps; `StampedEntity` gives create and modify.

actor.title: Tell the data layer who is working
actor.note: Register it as scoped. `IpAddress` and `SessionId` are optional and go only into the change history.

after-save.title: What the stamps hold after a save
after-save.note: Creator, UTC time and a fresh version were filled in; the modify stamp is still empty.

after-edit.title: What changes after an edit
after-edit.note: The edit wrote `ModifiedBy` and the time two hours later. The attempt to change `CreateBy` was ignored.

remove.title: Remove keeps the row as deleted
remove.note: Normal queries no longer see it (0), but the row is still there, marked with who deleted it.

options.title: History, version token and text kept as is
options.note: All three are switches on the entity; nothing changes in the entity class.

normalize.title: Clean up text before it is saved
normalize.note: Runs on every saved string except properties marked `KeepText`.

type.ICreateStamp: When and by whom a row was created.
type.IModifyStamp: When and by whom a row was last changed.
type.ISoftDelete: A row that is marked deleted instead of removed.
type.ITracked: Create, modify and soft delete stamps together.
type.StampedEntity: A base class with create and modify stamps.
type.TrackedEntity: A base class with create, modify and soft delete stamps.
type.IDataActor: Who is behind a save. Your app implements it.

ICreateStamp.CreateDate: UTC time the row was created. Set once and never overwritten.
ICreateStamp.CreateBy: Id of the user who created the row.

IModifyStamp.ModifiedDate: UTC time of the last change; empty until the first edit.
IModifyStamp.ModifiedBy: Id of the user who changed the row last.

ISoftDelete.IsDeleted: True once the row is removed. Queries skip such rows.
ISoftDelete.DeletedBy: Id of the user who deleted the row.

StampedEntity.CreateDate: UTC time the row was created.
StampedEntity.ModifiedDate: UTC time of the last change.

TrackedEntity.IsDeleted: True once the row is removed.
TrackedEntity.DeletedBy: Id of the user who deleted the row.

IDataActor.Id: The user's id, written into the stamps. Null leaves them empty.
IDataActor.Name: The user's display name, written into history rows.
IDataActor.IpAddress: The client address, written only into history rows. Optional; personal data, never logged.
IDataActor.SessionId: The session, written only into history rows. Optional.

concurrency.title: Two people, one row
concurrency.summary: With `Versioned()`, the second person to save an old copy gets `data.changed` instead of silently erasing the first person's work.

1.title: Silent overwrite
1.text: Without protection, the later save erases the earlier one unnoticed.

2.title: Version token
2.text: `Versioned()` adds a `Version` Guid that changes on every save.

3.title: Conflict result
3.text: A stale save stops with `data.changed` and writes nothing.

4.title: Any database
4.text: The same token works on every database package.

1.title: The problem
1.text: Sara and Reza open the same customer. Sara saves first. Without protection, Reza's save would overwrite Sara's change and nobody would notice.

2.title: How it works
2.text:
`Versioned()` adds a `Version` Guid that changes on every save, and the save checks that the version in the database is still the one you loaded.

If it is not, the save stops and returns `Conflict` with the code `data.changed`; nothing is written. Batch updates refresh the version too.

3.title: What to do next
3.text:
What to do next is a business decision: show the user the new data and let them try again, or reload and re-apply the change automatically when that is safe.

The same token works on every database package, so your model does not change when the database does.

conflict.title: What the second person gets
conflict.note: Sara's save succeeds; Reza's returns `Conflict` and `data.changed`, and his change is not written.

retry.title: Reload and try once more
retry.note: Only do this when re-applying the change is safe; otherwise ask the user.

audit.title: Change history
audit.summary: Call `Audit()` on an entity and every insert, change and delete leaves a row with the old and new values.

1.title: Change history
1.text: `ApplyAudit()` and `Audit()` write one `AuditRecord` per changed row.

2.title: Old and new
2.text: Each changed field keeps its old and new value.

3.title: Never recorded
3.text: Stamps, version and sensitive names are never written.

1.title: Turning it on
1.text:
When someone asks who changed a price and what it was before, the change history answers. Add the table with `modelBuilder.ApplyAudit()` and call `Audit()` on the entities you care about.

If an entity calls `Audit()` but `ApplyAudit` is missing, the save throws so you notice at once.

2.title: What is written
2.text:
Each save then writes one `AuditRecord` per changed row: what happened, which row, who, when, from which app, and each changed field with its old and new value.

A soft delete is recorded as a delete. Values are written the same way on every machine (invariant culture). A new row whose id comes from the database gets its real id in the history within the same transaction.

3.title: What is never written
3.text: Some things are never written: the stamp columns, the version token, sensitive names such as `Password`, `PasswordHash`, `Token` and `Secret`, and properties marked `[NoAudit]`.

4.title: Cleaning up
4.text: Old history is removed with `PurgeAuditsAsync`, in bounded batches, from a scheduled job.

trail.title: The history after an insert and an edit
trail.note: One row per change. The edit records only the field that actually changed.

secret.title: Keep a field out of the history
secret.note: `PasswordHash` is skipped by its name, `Notes` by the attribute.

history.title: Read the history of one row
history.note: The key is the primary key as text; a composite key is joined with `|`.

purge.title: Remove old history
purge.note: Up to 20 batches of 5000 rows per call, so it never holds a long lock.

table.title: Choose the table name
table.note: The default is `Audits` with no schema.

type.AuditRecord: One recorded change of one row.
type.AuditChange: One field with its old and new value.
type.AuditEx: Setting up the history table and removing old rows.
type.NoAuditAttribute: Keeps a property out of the history.

AuditRecord.AppCode: Which app made the change, from `EFCoreOptions.AppCode`.
AuditRecord.EntityKey: The changed row's key as text.
AuditRecord.IpAddress: Their address, if your `IDataActor` gives one.
AuditRecord.SessionId: Their session, if your `IDataActor` gives one.
AuditRecord.Changes: The changed fields, stored as JSON.

AuditChange.Old: The value before, or null for an insert.
AuditChange.New: The value after, or null for a delete.

AuditAction.Deleted: The row was deleted or soft deleted.

AuditEx.ApplyAudit: Adds the history table to the model, with indexes for entity, user and time.
AuditEx.PurgeAuditsAsync: Removes history older than the given days and returns how many rows went. 730 days by default.
AuditEx.RetentionDays: The default retention: 730 days, two years.

paging.title: Paging and reading in bulk
paging.summary: Page by number for screens, continue after a cursor for long lists, and stream when you need every row.

1.title: Page by number
1.text: `PageAsync` reads one page by its number.

2.title: Cursor paging
2.text: `PageAfterAsync` continues after the last row and stays fast.

3.title: Streaming
3.text: `StreamAsync` reads a whole table in batches of 5000.

4.title: Two rules
4.text: Sort by something unique and respect `MaxPageSize`.

1.title: Page by number
1.text:
Loading a whole table to show twenty rows is slow and wastes memory. `PageAsync` reads one page by number.

With `count: true` it also counts all rows so the screen can show 'page 3 of 5'. With `count: false` it reads one extra row and only tells you whether there is a next page, which is far cheaper on big tables.

2.title: Deep pages and cursors
2.text:
Page numbers get slow deep into a large table, because the database still walks past the skipped rows. `PageAfterAsync` avoids that: it continues right after the last row you saw, using a sort key and an id so rows with the same date are never skipped.

It gives you `Next`, a short cursor to send back for the following page. A cursor that cannot be read simply fails to decode; treat it as a bad request.

3.title: Whole table
3.text: `StreamAsync` reads a whole table in batches of 5000 for exports and jobs.

4.title: Two rules
4.text: Always sort by something unique (`OrderBy(name, type)` adds the key for you). Remember that page size is capped by `EFCoreOptions.MaxPageSize`.

offset.title: Page by number, with a total
offset.note: Use this for screens with page numbers.

page-numbers.title: What the page info tells you
page-numbers.note: With a total you get the page count; without one you only know whether more rows exist.

no-count.title: Page by number without counting
no-count.note: Good for 'load more' buttons on big tables.

keyset.title: Continue after a cursor
keyset.note: The cursor is not signed. It only says where to start, and its values go to SQL as parameters, so a forged cursor can only move the window.

cursor.title: Make and read a cursor
cursor.note: Text that is not a cursor returns false instead of throwing.

stream.title: Read every row for an export
stream.note: The key must be unique, for example the id. Progress reports how many rows were read so far.

type.KeysetPage{T}: One page and the cursor of the next page.
type.PageCursor: Turns the last row's keys into a short text and back.

KeysetPage{T}.Next: The cursor for the next page, or null on the last page.

PageCursor.Encode: Makes a URL-safe cursor from a key and an id.
PageCursor.TryDecode: Reads a cursor back. False for empty, too long or broken text.
PageCursor.MaxLength: The longest cursor that is accepted: 512 characters.

batches.title: Changing many rows at once
batches.summary: Update or delete thousands of rows in batches of 1000, each batch short, with stamps and history kept right.

1.title: Batches of 1000
1.text: Keys are picked 1000 at a time so others keep working.

2.title: Two update forms
2.text: Setters are fast SQL; `Action<T>` loads and saves.

3.title: Own transactions
3.text: Each batch is a short transaction; `atomicAll: true` makes it all-or-nothing.

4.title: Safe start
4.text: A batch refuses to start with unsaved changes.

1.title: How batches work
1.text:
One big UPDATE over a large table can lock it for minutes, and loading every row into memory can run out of it. The batch methods pick the matching keys 1000 at a time and work on each batch, so other users keep working.

For entities without history they send one SQL statement per batch and fill in the stamps themselves. For entities with `Audit()` they load each batch and save it, so every row gets its history entry.

2.title: Update and delete
2.text:
`BatchUpdateAsync` has two forms: with setters it is fast and SQL-only, and it refuses audited entities because the history needs the old values. With an `Action<T>` it loads and saves, slower but complete.

`BatchDeleteAsync` on a soft-delete entity marks rows deleted, like `Remove`.

3.title: Transactions and results
3.text:
Each batch is its own short transaction; pass `atomicAll: true` to make the whole job all-or-nothing when it is small.

The result is `data.deleted` or `data.batchDone` with the number of rows, or `data.notFound` when nothing matched. A batch refuses to start while the context has unsaved changes, so they are not saved by accident.

soft-delete.title: Soft delete many rows
soft-delete.note: Deleted and modified stamps are set in the same statement.

setters.title: Update with one statement per batch
setters.note: Fast. Not allowed for audited entities.

apply.title: Update by loading and saving
apply.note: Slower, but history, stamps and version work like a normal save.

atomic.title: All batches or none
atomic.note: Only for small jobs; a long transaction makes other users wait.

transactions.title: Transactions
transactions.summary: Put steps that must succeed together into `TranAsync`; it commits only when your work returns success.

1.title: All or nothing
1.text: `TranAsync` groups several steps; a failure rolls everything back.

2.title: Safe retry
2.text: On a temporary problem the whole function runs again.

3.title: Nesting
3.text: An inner `TranAsync` joins the outer one.

4.title: Keep it short
4.text: Send email or call services only after the commit.

1.title: When to use it
1.text:
A single `SaveAsync` is already all-or-nothing. You need `TranAsync` when several steps belong together, such as checking a customer and saving an invoice.

Write the work as a function that returns an `OSResult`. A successful result commits; a failed result, an exception or a cancellation rolls everything back, and nothing half-done stays.

2.title: Retries and errors
2.text:
If the database reports a temporary problem, the whole function runs again from a clean start, so load what you need inside it, not before. Database errors inside the work stop it and come back from `TranAsync` as the usual `data.*` result.

A `TranAsync` inside another one joins the outer one: only the outer one commits, and if an inner step fails, the whole unit rolls back.

3.title: TranOptions and Verify
3.text:
`TranOptions` sets the isolation level (Read committed by default), a timeout for this unit, a name for the logs, and `Verify`.

`Verify` matters in one rare case: the commit succeeded but the connection dropped before the answer came back. EF then asks your `Verify` whether the data is there; without it, the work could run twice, which can insert rows twice when their ids come from the database.

4.title: Good habits
4.text: Keep transactions short and send email or call other services only after the commit.

order.title: Check and save as one unit
order.note: Returning a failed result rolls back; the invoice is never saved without the check.

nested.title: A transaction inside a transaction
nested.note: The inner call joins the outer one. Only the outer one commits.

options.title: Isolation, timeout, name and commit check
options.note: `Verify` answers whether the commit really happened.

after-commit.title: Send the email after the commit
after-commit.note: If the email were inside and the transaction retried, the customer would get it twice.

type.TranOptions: How one transaction runs: isolation, timeout, name and commit check.

TranOptions.Isolation: The isolation level. Read committed by default; Snapshot and Serializable when you need them.
TranOptions.Timeout: The command timeout for this unit only; restored afterwards.
TranOptions.Verify: Called when the commit fails with a temporary error; return true if the data is already there.
TranOptions.Name: A name for the slow-transaction log. At most 100 characters.

errors.title: Errors and messages
errors.summary: A failed save returns a clear code, a status and the field that caused it, never a raw database exception.

1.title: Stable codes
1.text: A save never throws for a known database problem; the result carries a code.

2.title: Field names
2.text: `Errors` names the field for duplicate, required, too long and missing reference.

3.title: Localized messages
3.text: Messages come from your `IStringLocalizer` if you register one.

4.title: Safe details
4.text: Values, connection strings and server names never appear.

1.title: Why codes
1.text:
A raw database error is useless to a user and can leak table names and values. Here a save never throws for a known database problem. The database package recognizes its own error numbers and the result carries one stable code.

Programming mistakes, such as saving on a read-only context, still throw.

2.title: Error codes
2.text:
`data.duplicate` when a unique value is taken (Conflict), `data.inUse` when a row is still referenced and cannot be deleted (Conflict), `data.missingRef` when a related row does not exist (Invalid), `data.required` and `data.tooLong` (Invalid), `data.changed` when someone else saved first (Conflict).

`data.busy` for a deadlock, lock or timeout that did not clear after retries (Unavailable), `data.offline` when the database cannot be reached (Unavailable), and `data.error` for anything else.

For duplicate, required, too long and missing reference, `Errors` names the field. On success the codes are `data.saved`, `data.unchanged`, `data.deleted`, `data.notFound` and `data.batchDone`.

3.title: Messages and privacy
3.text:
Messages come from your `IStringLocalizer` if you register one: first the key `code.Entity.Property`, then `code`; otherwise a short English sentence.

Every error has a `TraceId`; the details go to the log and to `IErrorSink`, while values, connection strings and server names never appear in a result or a log.

duplicate.title: What a duplicate value returns
duplicate.note: Status, code, one field error for `Name`, and the default English message.

unchanged.title: Saving with nothing to save
unchanged.note: Not an error: `data.unchanged` tells you nothing was written.

handle.title: Turn a result into an answer for the user
handle.note: Decide on the code, never on the message text.

codes.title: All error codes
codes.note: These are also the keys for your translations.

localize.title: Use your own messages
localize.note: Any registered `IStringLocalizer` works, for example OS.Locale.

type.DataCodes: The stable result codes, and the name of the soft delete filter.

DataCodes.SoftDeleteFilter: The name of the query filter that hides deleted rows.
DataCodes.Duplicate: A unique value is already used.
DataCodes.InUse: The row is still referenced by other rows.
DataCodes.MissingRef: A related row does not exist.
DataCodes.TooLong: A value is too long or out of range.
DataCodes.Changed: Someone else saved this row first.
DataCodes.Busy: Deadlock, lock or timeout; try again.
DataCodes.Saved: The save worked; counts are in the data.
DataCodes.Deleted: A batch delete worked; the count is in the data.
DataCodes.BatchDone: A batch update worked; the count is in the data.

dates.title: Dates and time zones
dates.summary: Store `DateTimeOffset` in UTC everywhere; each database package keeps it so it sorts and compares correctly.

1.title: One rule
1.text: Use `DateTimeOffset`, store UTC, show local time only at the end.

2.title: UTC stamps
2.text: Stamps and history use UTC from `TimeProvider`.

3.title: Per database
3.text: Each package stores the value the way that works best there.

4.title: Database filtering
4.text: Filtering and sorting by date run in the database.

1.title: The rule
1.text:
Mixing local times from different servers and users makes reports wrong. The rule is simple: use `DateTimeOffset`, store UTC, and turn it into local time only when you show it.

The stamps and the change history already use UTC from `TimeProvider`, and in tests you can register your own clock.

2.title: Each database
2.text:
Each database package stores the value in the way that works best there. SQLite keeps UTC ticks, a number, because SQLite cannot compare dates. SQL Server keeps `datetimeoffset` as is.

PostgreSQL turns every value to UTC before writing, because `timestamptz` accepts only offset zero. MySQL keeps UTC `datetime(6)`, so fractional seconds are not lost.

In all of them the value comes back as UTC, and filtering and sorting by date run in the database.

utc.title: The same moment, written in UTC
utc.note: The offset changes, the moment does not: the two values are equal.

range.title: Filter and sort by date
range.note: Runs in SQL on every database package.

clock.title: Use your own clock
clock.note: Register it before `AddOSEFCore`; a fake clock makes stamp times predictable in tests.

migrations.title: Schema changes and naming
migrations.summary: You run migrations with the normal EF tools; the history table and snake_case names are settings.

1.title: Visible migrations
1.text: OS.EFCore does not hide migrations from you.

2.title: Production script
2.text: Generate an idempotent script, review it, run it in deployment.

3.title: Off by default
3.text: `MigrateOnStart` is off because two instances could both change the schema.

4.title: Snake case
4.text: `ApplySnakeCaseName` renames to snake_case, for new databases only.

1.title: Development and production
1.text:
OS.EFCore does not hide migrations from you. Create them with `dotnet ef migrations add Name` and apply them with `dotnet ef database update` during development.

For production, generate a script with `dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent`, review it, and run it as part of your deployment.

2.title: Migrating on start
2.text:
`MigrateOnStart` applies pending migrations when the app starts; it is off by default, because two app instances starting at the same time could both try to change the schema.

`HistoryTable` and `HistorySchema` rename EF's migrations history table.

3.title: Snake case names
3.text:
`ApplySnakeCaseName` turns table, column, key and index names into snake_case, which is common on PostgreSQL.

Call it at the end of `OnModelCreating`, and only for a new database: on an existing one it would rename everything.

history.title: History table and migrations at start-up
history.note: Leave `MigrateOnStart` off unless exactly one instance runs.

naming.title: Turn on snake_case names
naming.note: Names you set yourself with `ToTable` or `HasColumnName` are kept.

NamingEx.ApplySnakeCaseName: Renames tables, columns, keys and indexes to snake_case, keeping names you set explicitly.
NamingEx.ToSnake: Converts one PascalCase name to snake_case.

faq.title: Common questions
faq.summary: Short answers to the problems people run into most.

1.title: Nothing saved
1.text: You probably read with `Entity<T>()`; use `ForUpdate<T>()` or `Patch`.

2.title: Row still there
2.text: Soft delete is intended; `IgnoreSoftDelete()` shows such rows.

3.title: Result codes
3.text: `data.changed`, `data.busy` and `data.error` each have a clear next step.

4.title: Stamps and paging
4.text: Register `IDataActor` as scoped and sort by something unique.

1.title: Saves that do nothing
1.text:
I changed an entity and saved, but nothing happened. You probably read it with `Entity<T>()`, which does not track changes; load it with `ForUpdate<T>()`, or use `Patch` for an object from a form.

I deleted a row but it is still in the table. The entity has soft delete; that is intended, and `IgnoreSoftDelete()` shows such rows.

2.title: Error codes
2.text:
My save returns `data.changed`. Someone else saved the same row after you loaded it; reload and let the user decide.

My save returns `data.busy`. The database was locked or slow and the retries did not help; try again later, and keep transactions short.

My save returns `data.error`. The database package did not recognize the error; the `TraceId` in the result finds the details in the log.

3.title: Batches, stamps, paging
3.text:
A batch says it cannot run. Save or clear pending changes first, and use the `Action<T>` form of `BatchUpdateAsync` for audited entities.

The stamps are empty. Register your `IDataActor` as scoped; without it the user columns stay empty.

Paging repeats or skips rows. Sort by something unique; `OrderBy(name, type)` and `PageAfterAsync` already do.

4.title: Connection string
4.text: Where does my connection string go? In user secrets, environment variables or a key vault, never in source or in a log.

tracking.title: Why a change was not saved
tracking.note: The first change was on an untracked entity, so nothing was saved; the second used `ForUpdate`.

still-there.title: Why a deleted row is still in the table
still-there.note: Normal queries see 0 rows; with `IgnoreSoftDelete` the deleted row is still there.
